\title{Consistency of the relations of $G_{\mathfrak m}$: a machine-checked proof that no generator collapses}
\date{}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
The group $G_{\mathfrak m}$ is given by generators $H_1(s),H_2(s),X_{-1}(u),Y_{-1}(u),X_{\ell,jk}(u),Y_{\ell,jk}(u)$ and a list of relations. The authors asked whether these relations force some generator to be trivial. The formal proof shows that they do not: every generator family survives, and no relation was removed or modified. The proof uses the full index set (no constraint $j=2\ell+1$), keeps relation (Im:2), and allows an arbitrary function $c\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$. Non-triviality comes from explicit homomorphisms. The real generators are detected by a homomorphism to $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb C)$. Each imaginary generator is detected by a homomorphism to the linear automorphism group of $\mathbb C[X_0,X_1,Z]$, in which the imaginary generators act as transvections between two suitably chosen monomials.
\end{abstract}

\section{Statement}

Let $c(j)$ denote the coefficient of $q^j$ in the modular function
\[
J(q)=\sum_{j\ge -1}c(j)q^j=\frac1q+196884\,q+21493760\,q^2+\cdots .
\]
Put
\[
E=\{(\ell,j,k)\mid j\in\N,\ 1\le k\le c(j),\ 0\le \ell<j\}
\]
and
\[
c_{\ell j}:=(-1)^{\ell+1}\binom{j-1}{\ell}(\ell+1)(j-\ell).
\]
The group $\Gm$ is generated by the symbols
\[
H_1(s),\ H_2(s),\ X_{-1}(u),\ Y_{-1}(u),\ X_{\ell,jk}(u),\ Y_{\ell,jk}(u)\qquad (s\in\C^\times,\ u\in\C,\ (\ell,j,k)\in E).
\]
It is subject to the following relations, for all $s,t\in\C^\times$, $u,v\in\C$ and $(\ell,j,k),(m,p,q)\in E$:
\begin{align*}
\tag{Re:0} \wt_{-1}(s)&:=X_{-1}(s)Y_{-1}(-s^{-1})X_{-1}(s),\qquad \wt_{-1}:=\wt_{-1}(1),\\
\tag{H:1a} H_1(s)H_1(t)&=H_1(st),\\
\tag{H:1b} H_2(s)H_2(t)&=H_2(st),\\
\tag{H:2} H_1(s)H_2(t)&=H_2(t)H_1(s),\\
\tag{Re:1a} X_{-1}(u)X_{-1}(v)&=X_{-1}(u+v),\\
\tag{Re:1b} Y_{-1}(u)Y_{-1}(v)&=Y_{-1}(u+v),\\
\tag{Re:2} Y_{-1}(-t)X_{-1}(s)Y_{-1}(t)&=X_{-1}(-t^{-1})Y_{-1}(-t^2s)X_{-1}(t^{-1}),\\
\tag{Re:3} \wt_{-1}(s)\wt_{-1}&=H_1(-s)H_2(-s^{-1}),\\
\tag{Re:4a} \wt_{-1}X_{-1}(u)\wt_{-1}^{-1}&=Y_{-1}(-u),\\
\tag{Re:4b} \wt_{-1}Y_{-1}(u)\wt_{-1}^{-1}&=X_{-1}(-u),\\
\tag{Re:5a} \wt_{-1}H_1(s)\wt_{-1}^{-1}&=H_2(s),\\
\tag{Re:5b} \wt_{-1}H_2(s)\wt_{-1}^{-1}&=H_1(s),\\
\tag{Re:6a} H_1(s)X_{-1}(u)H_1(s)^{-1}&=X_{-1}(su),\\
\tag{Re:6b} H_2(s)X_{-1}(u)H_2(s)^{-1}&=X_{-1}(s^{-1}u),\\
\tag{Re:6c} H_1(s)Y_{-1}(u)H_1(s)^{-1}&=Y_{-1}(s^{-1}u),\\
\tag{Re:6d} H_2(s)Y_{-1}(u)H_2(s)^{-1}&=Y_{-1}(su),\\
\tag{Im:1a} X_{\ell,jk}(u)X_{\ell,jk}(v)&=X_{\ell,jk}(u+v),\\
\tag{Im:1b} Y_{\ell,jk}(u)Y_{\ell,jk}(v)&=Y_{\ell,jk}(u+v),\\
\tag{Im:2} Y_{\ell,jk}(-t)X_{\ell,jk}(s)Y_{\ell,jk}(t)&=X_{\ell,jk}\Bigl(\tfrac{-t^{-1}}{c_{\ell j}}\Bigr)Y_{\ell,jk}(-c_{\ell j}t^2s)X_{\ell,jk}\Bigl(\tfrac{t^{-1}}{c_{\ell j}}\Bigr),\\
\tag{Im:6a} H_1(s)X_{\ell,jk}(u)H_1(s)^{-1}&=X_{\ell,jk}(s^{\ell+1}u),\\
\tag{Im:6b} H_2(s)X_{\ell,jk}(u)H_2(s)^{-1}&=X_{\ell,jk}(s^{j-\ell}u),\\
\tag{Im:6c} H_1(s)Y_{\ell,jk}(u)H_1(s)^{-1}&=Y_{\ell,jk}(s^{-(\ell+1)}u),\\
\tag{Im:6d} H_2(s)Y_{\ell,jk}(u)H_2(s)^{-1}&=Y_{\ell,jk}(s^{-(j-\ell)}u),\\
\tag{U:1a} (X_{-1}(u),X_{j-1,jk}(v))&=1,\\
\tag{U:1b} (Y_{-1}(u),Y_{j-1,jk}(v))&=1,\\
\tag{U:1c} (Y_{-1}(u),X_{0,jk}(v))&=1,\\
\tag{U:1d} (X_{-1}(u),Y_{0,jk}(v))&=1,\\
\tag{U:2} (X_{\ell,jk}(u),Y_{m,pq}(v))&=1\quad\text{if } j\ne p\text{ or } k\ne q\text{ or } |\ell-m|>1,\\
\tag{U:4a} \wt_{-1}X_{\ell,jk}(u)\wt_{-1}^{-1}&=X_{j-1-\ell,jk}((-1)^{\ell}u),\\
\tag{U:4b} \wt_{-1}Y_{\ell,jk}(u)\wt_{-1}^{-1}&=Y_{j-1-\ell,jk}((-1)^{j-\ell-1}u),\\
\tag{U:5a} Y_{-1}(s)&=X_{-1}(s^{-1})H_1(-s^{-1})H_2(-s)\wt_{-1}X_{-1}(s^{-1}).
\end{align*}

\begin{theorem}
The relations of $\Gm$ are consistent: no generator is forced to be trivial. In $\Gm$ the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item $X_{-1}(u)\ne1$ and $Y_{-1}(u)\ne1$ for $u\ne0$;
\item $H_1(s)\ne1$ and $H_2(s)\ne1$ for $s\ne1$;
\item $X_{\ell,jk}(u)\ne1$ and $Y_{\ell,jk}(u)\ne1$ for every $(\ell,j,k)\in E$ and $u\ne0$.
\end{itemize}
\end{theorem}

\paragraph{Answer to the authors' question.}
The relations are consistent. No generator family collapses: all six families $X_{-1}$, $Y_{-1}$, $H_1$, $H_2$, $X_{\ell,jk}$, $Y_{\ell,jk}$ survive. The formal proof uses the relations exactly as listed:
\begin{itemize}
\item the full index set $E$, without the constraint $j=2\ell+1$;
\item relation (Im:2), which is kept;
\item an arbitrary function $c\colon\N\to\N$ in place of the coefficients of $J$.
\end{itemize}
No relation was removed, weakened or added.

\section{Formalization}

The formalization uses Mathlib's free groups ($\mathrm{FreeGroup}$), groups given by generators and relators ($\mathrm{PresentedGroup}$, the quotient of the free group by the normal closure of a set of relators), and the universal property $\mathrm{PresentedGroup.toGroup}$. The universal property says that a map from the generators to a group $T$ that sends every relator to $1$ induces a homomorphism $\Gm\to T$ extending it. The formalization also uses multivariate polynomials ($\mathrm{MvPolynomial}$) and $\GL_2(\C)$.

Throughout, $c\colon\N\to\N$ is an arbitrary function. It plays the role of the coefficient function of $J$, whose actual values are never used.

\paragraph{The index set.}
$E_c$ is the set of triples $(\ell,j,k)$ of natural numbers with $1\le k$, $k\le c(j)$ and $\ell<j$. In particular $j\ge1$. Two indices are equal exactly when their triples are equal. For $e\in E_c$ we write $\ell(e),j(e),k(e)$ for its components.

\paragraph{Reflection of an index.}
For $e=(\ell,j,k)\in E_c$ put $e^*:=(j-1-\ell,\,j,\,k)$. This lies in $E_c$, because $j-1-\ell<j$.

\paragraph{Generators.}
$\Gen_c$ is the disjoint union of the following symbol families:
\begin{itemize}
\item $H_1(s)$ and $H_2(s)$ for $s\in\C^\times$;
\item $X_{-1}(u)$ and $Y_{-1}(u)$ for $u\in\C$;
\item $X_e(u)$ and $Y_e(u)$ for $e\in E_c$, $u\in\C$.
\end{itemize}
For $e=(\ell,j,k)$, $X_e(u)$ stands for $X_{\ell,jk}(u)$ and $Y_e(u)$ for $Y_{\ell,jk}(u)$. The parameter of $H_i$ is a unit of $\C$, so $-s$ and $s^{-1}$ are computed in $\C^\times$.

\paragraph{The constant $c_{\ell j}$.}
For $\ell,j\in\N$,
\[
c_{\ell j}=(-1)^{\ell+1}\binom{j-1}{\ell}(\ell+1)\,(j-\ell)\in\C .
\]
Here $j-1$ is truncated subtraction in $\N$; it is irrelevant on $E_c$, where $j\ge1$. The factor $j-\ell$ is computed in $\C$.

\paragraph{Abbreviations in the free group.}
In the free group $F(\Gen_c)$ we write $H_1(s)$, $H_2(s)$, $X_{-1}(u)$, $Y_{-1}(u)$, $X_e(u)$, $Y_e(u)$ for the images of the symbols. We also use the following abbreviations:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\wt_{-1}(s)=X_{-1}(s)\,Y_{-1}(-s^{-1})\,X_{-1}(s)$ for $s\in\C^\times$, as in (Re:0);
\item $\wt_{-1}=\wt_{-1}(1)=X_{-1}(1)Y_{-1}(-1)X_{-1}(1)$;
\item $(a,b)=aba^{-1}b^{-1}$, the commutator.
\end{itemize}
These are abbreviations, not generators.

\paragraph{The relators.}
The set $\mathcal R_c\subseteq F(\Gen_c)$ is an inductive predicate with one constructor per relation family. A relation $a=b$ is encoded as the relator $ab^{-1}$; a commutator relation $(a,b)=1$ as the relator $(a,b)$. The families are (H:1a), (H:1b), (H:2), (Re:1a)--(Re:6d), (Im:1a), (Im:1b), (Im:2), (Im:6a)--(Im:6d), (U:1a)--(U:1d), (U:2), (U:4a), (U:4b), (U:5a). Each is imposed for all $s,t\in\C^\times$, $u,v\in\C$ and all indices in $E_c$, with the following precise forms.
\begin{itemize}
\item (Re:2) and (Im:2) are imposed for $s,t\in\C^\times$. In (Im:2) the constant is $c_{\ell(e)j(e)}$.
\item (Im:6c) reads $H_1(s)Y_e(u)H_1(s)^{-1}=Y_e((s^{-1})^{\ell+1}u)$, and (Im:6d) reads $H_2(s)Y_e(u)H_2(s)^{-1}=Y_e((s^{-1})^{j-\ell}u)$.
\item (U:1a), (U:1b) are imposed for those $e$ with $\ell(e)=j(e)-1$; (U:1c), (U:1d) for those with $\ell(e)=0$.
\item (U:2) is imposed for all $e,f\in E_c$ with $j(e)\ne j(f)$, or $k(e)\ne k(f)$, or $|\ell(e)-\ell(f)|>1$, the absolute value taken in $\Z$.
\item (U:4a) reads $\wt_{-1}X_e(u)\wt_{-1}^{-1}=X_{e^*}((-1)^{\ell}u)$, and (U:4b) reads $\wt_{-1}Y_e(u)\wt_{-1}^{-1}=Y_{e^*}((-1)^{j-\ell-1}u)$.
\end{itemize}
No constraint $j=2\ell+1$ is imposed, and (Im:2) is present.

The target statement asserts, for every $c\colon\N\to\N$, the conjunction of six statements in $\Gm(c)$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X_{-1}(u)\ne1$ for all $u\in\C$ with $u\ne0$;
\item $Y_{-1}(u)\ne1$ for all $u\in\C$ with $u\ne0$;
\item $H_1(s)\ne1$ for all $s\in\C^\times$ with $s\ne1$;
\item $H_2(s)\ne1$ for all $s\in\C^\times$ with $s\ne1$;
\item $X_e(u)\ne1$ for all $e\in E_c$ and $u\in\C$ with $u\ne0$;
\item $Y_e(u)\ne1$ for all $e\in E_c$ and $u\in\C$ with $u\ne0$.
\end{enumerate}
This is the theorem of the source with the following conventions:
\begin{itemize}
\item the function $c$ is arbitrary, so the result holds in particular for the coefficients of $J$ (restricted to $j\in\N$, which is all that $E$ uses);
\item $\GL_2(-1)$ and $\C$ are $\GL_2(\C)$ and $\C$;
\item the relations are those listed above, with no change.
\end{itemize}
The theorem \leanname{solution}, proved at the end, has exactly this six-part statement.

The statement concerns each generator individually. It does not assert, for instance, that distinct symbols have distinct images.

\section{Proof}

\subsection{Overview}

The source gives no proof; the authors ask whether the relations are consistent. The formal proof answers this positively: each generator is shown to be non-trivial by mapping $\Gm(c)$ homomorphically to a group in which its image is visibly non-trivial.

\paragraph{Real part.}
Send the generators to $\GL_2(\C)$ by
\[
H_1(s)\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(s,1),\quad H_2(s)\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(1,s),\quad X_{-1}(u)\mapsto\mat1u01,\quad Y_{-1}(u)\mapsto\mat10u1,
\]
and send all $X_e(u),Y_e(u)$ to $1$. Every relator becomes the identity (\cref{lem:setting_real_part_nontrivial,lem:gm_gl2_rel_aux,lem:gm_gl2_rel}). Reading off one matrix entry gives the first four claims.

\paragraph{Imaginary part: the representation.}
Let $P=\C[X_0,X_1,Z]$ and let $\Aut(P)$ be its group of $\C$-linear automorphisms. The group $\GL_2(\C)$ acts on $P$ by algebra automorphisms $\rho(g)=\sigma_g$, defined by
\[
X_0\mapsto g_{11}X_0+g_{21}X_1,\qquad X_1\mapsto g_{12}X_0+g_{22}X_1,\qquad Z\mapsto\det(g)\,Z.
\]
Monomials are weight vectors: $\mathrm{diag}(a,b)$ multiplies $X_0^{m_0}X_1^{m_1}Z^{m_2}$ by $a^{m_0+m_2}b^{m_1+m_2}$. The Weyl matrix $\mat01{-1}0$ swaps $X_0$ and $X_1$ up to a sign. The unipotent matrices fix monomials not containing $X_1$ (respectively $X_0$).

For two distinct monomials $x^p,x^q$, the transvection $\tau_{p,q}(u)$ is the linear map
\[
v\mapsto v+u\,\cfx{q}{v}\,x^p,
\]
where $\cfx{q}{v}$ is the coefficient of $x^q$ in $v$.

\paragraph{Imaginary part: one homomorphism per index.}
For a fixed $e\in E_c$ we choose:
\begin{itemize}
\item monomials $p,q$ (for $e$) and $p',q'$ (for $e^*$);
\item scalars $\alpha,\beta,\alpha',\beta'$.
\end{itemize}
We then define a homomorphism $\Gm(c)\to\Aut(P)$ by:
\begin{itemize}
\item real generators act through $\rho$;
\item $X_e(u)\mapsto\tau_{p,q}(\alpha u)$ and $Y_e(u)\mapsto\tau_{q,p}(\beta u)$;
\item $X_{e^*}(u)\mapsto\tau_{p',q'}(\alpha' u)$ and $Y_{e^*}(u)\mapsto\tau_{q',p'}(\beta' u)$;
\item every other imaginary generator goes to $1$.
\end{itemize}
The relations hold under the following conditions, which are the hypotheses of the claim in the proof of the theorem.
\begin{itemize}
\item (Im:1): automatic (\cref{lem:gm_tau_add}).
\item (Im:2): holds if $\alpha\beta=c_{\ell j}$. Then $\tau_{p,q},\tau_{q,p}$ realize a rescaled copy of the $\mathrm{SL}_2$ identity (Re:2) on the plane spanned by $x^p,x^q$ (\cref{lem:gm_tau_sl2}).
\item (Im:6): holds if the weight of $x^p$ minus the weight of $x^q$ is $(\ell+1,\,j-\ell)$ (\cref{lem:gm_conj_diag}).
\item (U:4): holds if $p',q'$ are the swaps of $p,q$ and suitable sign conditions on $\alpha,\beta,\alpha',\beta'$ hold (\cref{lem:gm_conj_W}).
\item (U:1): holds if certain exponents of $p,q$ vanish, so that the relevant monomials are fixed by the unipotent elements (\cref{lem:gm_comm_ux,lem:gm_comm_uy}).
\item (U:2): holds if $p\ne p'$ and $q\ne q'$ whenever $|\ell-\ell(e^*)|>1$ (\cref{lem:gm_tau_comm}).
\end{itemize}
The bookkeeping that extends these properties from the two indices $e,e^*$ to all of $E_c$ (where the representation is trivial) is done by the generic \cref{lem:gm_fam_add,lem:gm_fam_conj,lem:gm_fam_weyl,lem:gm_fam_comm1,lem:gm_fam_U2,lem:gm_fam_XY}. These are assembled by \cref{lem:gm_rel_of}. A non-trivial transvection is not the identity (\cref{lem:gm_tau_ne_one}), which gives the last two claims.

\paragraph{Choice of monomials.}
The monomials are chosen according to the sign of $2\ell+1-j$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $j\le2\ell$, take
\[
x^p=X_0Z^{\ell},\qquad x^q=X_1^{2\ell-j},\qquad x^{p'}=X_1Z^{\ell},\qquad x^{q'}=X_0^{2\ell-j},
\]
with
\[
\alpha=1,\quad\beta=c_{\ell j},\quad\alpha'=(-1)^{\ell+1},\quad\beta'=-c_{\ell j}(-1)^{j-\ell-1}.
\]
\item If $j=2\ell+1$ (so $e^*=e$), take $x^p=x^{p'}=(X_0X_1)^{\ell}Z$, $x^q=x^{q'}=1$, $\alpha=\alpha'=1$ and $\beta=\beta'=c_{\ell j}$.
\item If $j\ge2\ell+2$, apply the first case to $e^*$, using $e^{**}=e$.
\end{itemize}
The arithmetic needed for these choices is in \cref{lem:gm_pos_cst,lem:gm_pos_signX,lem:gm_pos_signY,lem:gm_pos_signX',lem:gm_pos_signY',lem:gm_cst_ne_zero,lem:gm_pow_inv_mul}.

\paragraph{Notation and standing conventions for this section.}
For $m=(m_0,m_1,m_2)\in\N^3$ write $x^m=X_0^{m_0}X_1^{m_1}Z^{m_2}\in P$, and $\cfx{m}{f}$ for the coefficient of $x^m$ in $f\in P$. Exponent vectors are finitely supported functions on $\{0,1,2\}$, that is, elements of $\N^3$.

In $\Aut(P)$ the product is composition, $(\varphi\psi)(v)=\varphi(\psi(v))$, and $1$ is the identity.

For $g=\mat{g_{11}}{g_{12}}{g_{21}}{g_{22}}\in\GL_2(\C)$, let $\sigma_g$ be the $\C$-algebra endomorphism of $P$ with
\[
\sigma_g(X_0)=g_{11}X_0+g_{21}X_1,\qquad \sigma_g(X_1)=g_{12}X_0+g_{22}X_1,\qquad \sigma_g(Z)=\det(g)\,Z .
\]
We write
\[
\up(t)=\mat1t01,\qquad \lo(t)=\mat10t1,\qquad W=\mat01{-1}0 .
\]
Statements about elements $g\in\GL_2(\C)$ such as "$g=\up(t)$" refer to the underlying matrix.

Many lemmas carry two hypotheses on auxiliary data:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(R)] $\rho\colon\GL_2(\C)\to\Aut(P)$ is a group homomorphism with $\rho(g)(f)=\sigma_g(f)$ for all $g\in\GL_2(\C)$ and $f\in P$.
\item[(T)] $\tau$ assigns to every $p,q\in\N^3$ and $u\in\C$ an element $\tau_{p,q}(u)\in\Aut(P)$ such that, whenever $p\ne q$, $\tau_{p,q}(u)(v)=v+u\,\cfx{q}{v}\,x^p$ for all $u\in\C$ and $v\in P$.
\end{itemize}

For $F\colon\Gen_c\to T$ into a group $T$, $\overline F\colon F(\Gen_c)\to T$ denotes the homomorphism extending $F$.

In the generic lemmas, $T$ is a group, $e\in E_c$, and $G\colon E_c\times\C\to T$. We say that $G$ is \emph{supported at $e$ with values $A,A'$} (where $A,A'\colon\C\to T$) if:
\begin{itemize}
\item $G(e,u)=A(u)$ for all $u$;
\item $G(e^*,u)=A'(u)$ for all $u$;
\item $G(g,u)=1$ for all $u$ and all $g\ne e$, $g\ne e^*$.
\end{itemize}

The first lemma was supplied with the setting; we prove it here because it is a theorem.

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{setting_real_part_nontrivial}]\label{lem:setting_real_part_nontrivial}
Let $c\colon\N\to\N$ be arbitrary. In $\Gm(c)$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $X_{-1}(u)\ne1$ and $Y_{-1}(u)\ne1$ for every $u\in\C$ with $u\ne0$;
\item $H_1(s)\ne1$ and $H_2(s)\ne1$ for every $s\in\C^\times$ with $s\ne1$.
\end{itemize}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Define $f\colon\Gen_c\to\GL_2(\C)$ by
\[
f(H_1(s))=\mathrm{diag}(s,1),\quad f(H_2(s))=\mathrm{diag}(1,s),\quad f(X_{-1}(u))=\up(u),\quad f(Y_{-1}(u))=\lo(u),
\]
and $f(X_e(u))=f(Y_e(u))=1$. These matrices are invertible, with inverses $\mathrm{diag}(s^{-1},1)$, $\mathrm{diag}(1,s^{-1})$, $\up(-u)$ and $\lo(-u)$.

We check that $\overline f(r)=1$ for every relator $r$, family by family.

Under $f$ we have $\wt_{-1}(s)\mapsto\up(s)\lo(-s^{-1})\up(s)=\mat0s{-s^{-1}}0$, and in particular $\wt_{-1}\mapsto W$.
\begin{itemize}
\item (H:1a), (H:1b), (H:2): diagonal matrices multiply entrywise and commute.
\item (Re:1a), (Re:1b): $\up(u)\up(v)=\up(u+v)$ and $\lo(u)\lo(v)=\lo(u+v)$.
\item (Re:2): both $\lo(-t)\up(s)\lo(t)$ and $\up(-t^{-1})\lo(-t^2s)\up(t^{-1})$ equal $\mat{1+st}{s}{-st^2}{1-st}$.
\item (Re:3): $\mat0s{-s^{-1}}0W=\mathrm{diag}(-s,-s^{-1})$.
\item (Re:4a), (Re:4b): $W\up(u)W^{-1}=\lo(-u)$ and $W\lo(u)W^{-1}=\up(-u)$.
\item (Re:5a), (Re:5b): conjugation by $W$ interchanges $\mathrm{diag}(s,1)$ and $\mathrm{diag}(1,s)$.
\item (Re:6a)--(Re:6d): conjugating $\up(u)$ by $\mathrm{diag}(s,1)$ and $\mathrm{diag}(1,s)$ gives $\up(su)$ and $\up(s^{-1}u)$; conjugating $\lo(u)$ gives $\lo(s^{-1}u)$ and $\lo(su)$.
\item (U:5a): $\up(s^{-1})\,\mathrm{diag}(-s^{-1},-s)\,W\,\up(s^{-1})=\lo(s)$, since $\mathrm{diag}(-s^{-1},-s)W=\mat0{-s^{-1}}{s}0$.
\item All remaining families involve imaginary generators, which map to $1$. Their relators become $1\cdot1\cdot1^{-1}=1$, $h\cdot1\cdot h^{-1}=1$, or commutators with $1$.
\end{itemize}
By the universal property, $f$ induces a homomorphism $\varphi\colon\Gm(c)\to\GL_2(\C)$ with $\varphi(z)=f(z)$ on generators.

Suppose $X_{-1}(u)=1$. Then $\up(u)=1$, and the $(1,2)$ entry gives $u=0$. The same argument works for $Y_{-1}(u)$ with the $(2,1)$ entry. For $H_1(s)$ and $H_2(s)$, the $(1,1)$ and $(2,2)$ entries give $s=1$ in $\C$, hence in $\C^\times$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_gl2_rel_aux}]\label{lem:gm_gl2_rel_aux}
Let $c\colon\N\to\N$ and $f_0\colon\Gen_c\to\GL_2(\C)$ satisfy:
\begin{itemize}
\item $f_0(H_1(s))=\mathrm{diag}(s,1)$ and $f_0(H_2(s))=\mathrm{diag}(1,s)$ for all $s\in\C^\times$;
\item $f_0(X_{-1}(u))=\up(u)$ and $f_0(Y_{-1}(u))=\lo(u)$ for all $u\in\C$;
\item $f_0(X_e(u))=f_0(Y_e(u))=1$ for all $e\in E_c$ and $u\in\C$.
\end{itemize}
Then $\overline{f_0}(r)=1$ for every $r\in\mathcal R_c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both sides are algebra endomorphisms applied to $f$, so it suffices to compare them on $X_0,X_1,Z$. We have
\[
\sigma_g(\sigma_h(X_0))=h_{11}(g_{11}X_0+g_{21}X_1)+h_{21}(g_{12}X_0+g_{22}X_1)=(gh)_{11}X_0+(gh)_{21}X_1 .
\]
The computation for $X_1$ is similar. On $Z$, $\det h\det g=\det(gh)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_L_inv}]\label{lem:gm_L_inv}

\begin{proof}
Let $a=\cfx{q}{f}$. Since $p\ne q$, we have $\cfx{q}{\bigl(f+va\,x^p\bigr)}=a$. Hence the left side sends $f$ to
\[
f+va\,x^p+ua\,x^p=f+(u+v)a\,x^p=f .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_tau_add}]\label{lem:gm_tau_add}
Assume (T). For $p\ne q$ and $u,v\in\C$, $\tau_{p,q}(u)\tau_{p,q}(v)=\tau_{p,q}(u+v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $w\in P$, the map $\tau_{p,q}(v)$ does not change the coefficient of $x^q$, since $p\ne q$. Therefore
\[
\tau_{p,q}(u)\tau_{p,q}(v)w=w+v\,\cfx{q}{w}\,x^p+u\,\cfx{q}{w}\,x^p=\tau_{p,q}(u+v)w .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_tau_sl2}]\label{lem:gm_tau_sl2}
Assume (T). Let $p\ne q$ in $\N^3$, let $a,b,\kappa\in\C$ with $ab=\kappa$ and $\kappa\ne0$, and let $s,t\in\C^\times$. Then
\[
\tau_{q,p}(b(-t))\,\tau_{p,q}(as)\,\tau_{q,p}(bt)=\tau_{p,q}\bigl(a(-t^{-1}/\kappa)\bigr)\,\tau_{q,p}\bigl(b(-\kappa t^2s)\bigr)\,\tau_{p,q}\bigl(a\,t^{-1}/\kappa\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $v\in P$, $\tau_{p,q}(x)$ changes only the coefficient at $p$, replacing $c_p$ by $c_p+xc_q$. Similarly $\tau_{q,p}(x)$ replaces $c_q$ by $c_q+xc_p$. Thus all coefficients outside $\{p,q\}$ are unchanged by both sides. On the column vector $(c_p,c_q)$ the two maps act by $\up(x)$ and $\lo(x)$, and composition of maps corresponds to the product of matrices in the same order.

The claim therefore reduces to the matrix identity
\[
\lo(-bt)\,\up(as)\,\lo(bt)=\up\bigl(-(bt)^{-1}\bigr)\,\lo\bigl(-(bt)^2as\bigr)\,\up\bigl((bt)^{-1}\bigr),
\]
together with $-(bt)^{-1}=a(-t^{-1}/\kappa)$ and $-(bt)^2as=b(-\kappa t^2s)$, both of which use $ab=\kappa$. The matrix identity is the computation for (Re:2) in \cref{lem:setting_real_part_nontrivial}, with $s,t$ replaced by $as$ and $bt$; it requires only $bt\ne0$. Here $a,b\ne0$ because $\kappa\ne0$.

The formal proof compares the coefficient at each $m$, in the cases $m=p$, $m=q$, and $m\notin\{p,q\}$, by field arithmetic.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_tau_comm}]\label{lem:gm_tau_comm}
Assume (T). Let $p,q,p',q'\in\N^3$ with $p\ne q$, $p'\ne q'$, $p\ne p'$, $q\ne q'$. Then for all $u,v\in\C$,
\[
\tau_{p,q}(u)\tau_{q',p'}(v)=\tau_{q',p'}(v)\tau_{p,q}(u).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The map $\tau_{q',p'}(v)$ modifies only the coefficient at $q'\ne q$, and $\tau_{p,q}(u)$ modifies only the coefficient at $p\ne p'$. Hence each map leaves unchanged the coefficient that the other one reads. Both sides send $w$ to
\[
w+u\,\cfx{q}{w}\,x^p+v\,\cfx{p'}{w}\,x^{q'} .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
We have $\tau_{p,q}(u)(x^q)=x^q+u\,x^p$. Its coefficient at $p$ is $u\ne0$, while that of $x^q$ is $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_conj_tau}]\label{lem:gm_conj_tau}
Assume (T). Let $\varphi\in\Aut(P)$, let $p\ne q$ and $p'\ne q'$ in $\N^3$, and let $\mu,\nu\in\C$ satisfy:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\varphi(x^p)=\mu\,x^{p'}$;
\item $\cfx{q}{\varphi^{-1}(v)}=\nu\,\cfx{q'}{v}$ for all $v\in P$.
\end{itemize}
Then $\varphi\,\tau_{p,q}(u)\,\varphi^{-1}=\tau_{p',q'}(\mu\nu u)$ for every $u\in\C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By linearity of $\varphi$,
\[
\varphi\bigl(\varphi^{-1}v+u\,\cfx{q}{\varphi^{-1}v}\,x^p\bigr)=v+u\nu\,\cfx{q'}{v}\,\mu x^{p'}=\tau_{p',q'}(\mu\nu u)(v).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_rho_diag_monomial_aiprover_s0}]\label{lem:gm_rho_diag_monomial_aiprover_s0}
Assume (R). Let $g\in\GL_2(\C)$ with $g=\mathrm{diag}(a,b)$ for some $a,b\in\C$, and let $m\in\N^3$. Then
\[
\rho(g)(x^m)=a^{m_0}b^{m_1}(ab)^{m_2}\,x^m .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By (R), $\rho(g)=\sigma_g$, and $\sigma_g$ sends $X_0\mapsto aX_0$, $X_1\mapsto bX_1$ and $Z\mapsto abZ$. Since $\sigma_g$ is multiplicative, it sends $x^m$ to $(aX_0)^{m_0}(bX_1)^{m_1}(abZ)^{m_2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_coeff_rho_diag}]\label{lem:gm_coeff_rho_diag}
Assume (R). Let $g=\mathrm{diag}(a,b)\in\GL_2(\C)$, $q\in\N^3$ and $v\in P$. Then
\[
\cfx{q}{\rho(g)(v)}=a^{q_0}b^{q_1}(ab)^{q_2}\,\cfx{q}{v}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both sides are additive in $v$, so it suffices to treat $v=r\,x^m$. By \cref{lem:gm_rho_diag_monomial}, $\rho(g)(r x^m)=r\,a^{m_0}b^{m_1}(ab)^{m_2}x^m$. If $m=q$, the coefficients at $q$ agree. If $m\ne q$, both coefficients are $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_rho_W_monomial}]\label{lem:gm_rho_W_monomial}
Assume (R). Let $g\in\GL_2(\C)$ with $g=W$, and let $m,m'\in\N^3$ with $m'_0=m_1$, $m'_1=m_0$, $m'_2=m_2$. Then
\[
\rho(g)(x^m)=(-1)^{m_0}\,x^{m'} .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $g=W$, $\sigma_g$ sends $X_0\mapsto -X_1$, $X_1\mapsto X_0$ and $Z\mapsto Z$, since $\det W=1$. Hence
\[
x^m\mapsto(-X_1)^{m_0}X_0^{m_1}Z^{m_2}=(-1)^{m_0}x^{m'} .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_coeff_rho_W_inv}]\label{lem:gm_coeff_rho_W_inv}
Assume (R). Let $g=W$, and let $q,q'\in\N^3$ with $q'_0=q_1$, $q'_1=q_0$, $q'_2=q_2$. Then for every $v\in P$,
\[
\cfx{q}{\rho(g)^{-1}(v)}=(-1)^{q_0}\,\cfx{q'}{v}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We first show that $\cfx{q'}{\rho(g)(w)}=(-1)^{q_0}\cfx{q}{w}$ for all $w$. By additivity it suffices to take $w=a\,x^u$. By \cref{lem:gm_rho_W_monomial}, $\rho(g)(a x^u)=a(-1)^{u_0}x^{\bar u}$, where $\bar u=(u_1,u_0,u_2)$. Now $\bar u=q'$ if and only if $u=q$, and in that case $u_0=q_0$. This gives the identity.

Apply it to $w=\rho(g)^{-1}v$ and multiply by $(-1)^{q_0}$, using $((-1)^{q_0})^2=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_rho_ux_monomial_aiprover_s0}]\label{lem:gm_rho_ux_monomial_aiprover_s0}
Assume (R). Let $g=\up(u)$ for some $u\in\C$, and let $m\in\N^3$ with $m_1=0$. Then $\rho(g)(x^m)=x^m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $g=\up(u)$, $\sigma_g$ sends $X_0\mapsto X_0$, $X_1\mapsto uX_0+X_1$ and $Z\mapsto Z$, since $\det g=1$. A monomial without $X_1$ is therefore fixed.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv_kill}]\label{lem:gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv_kill}
Let $E_0$ be the $\C$-algebra endomorphism of $P$ with $X_0\mapsto0$, $X_1\mapsto X_1$, $Z\mapsto Z$. If $q\in\N^3$ satisfies $q_0=0$, then $\cfx{q}{E_0(f)}=\cfx{q}{f}$ for every $f\in P$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By additivity it suffices to take $f=a\,x^m$. If $m_0=0$, then $E_0(f)=f$. If $m_0>0$, then $E_0(f)=0$, and $m\ne q$ because $q_0=0$; so both coefficients are $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv_fix}]\label{lem:gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv_fix}
Assume (R), and let $g=\up(u)$. With $E_0$ as in \cref{lem:gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv_kill}, $E_0(\rho(g)(f))=E_0(f)$ for every $f\in P$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $g=\lo(u)$, $\sigma_g$ sends $X_0\mapsto X_0+uX_1$, $X_1\mapsto X_1$ and $Z\mapsto Z$. A monomial without $X_0$ is therefore fixed.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_coeff_rho_uy_inv_E}]\label{lem:gm_coeff_rho_uy_inv_E}
Let $E_1$ be the $\C$-algebra endomorphism of $P$ with $X_0\mapsto X_0$, $X_1\mapsto0$, $Z\mapsto Z$. If $q_1=0$, then $\cfx{q}{E_1(f)}=\cfx{q}{f}$ for every $f\in P$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_coeff_rho_uy_inv}]\label{lem:gm_coeff_rho_uy_inv}
Assume (R). Let $g=\lo(u)$ and $q\in\N^3$ with $q_1=0$. Then $\cfx{q}{\rho(g)^{-1}(v)}=\cfx{q}{v}$ for every $v\in P$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$E_1\circ\sigma_g=E_1$, because $E_1(X_0+uX_1)=X_0$, $E_1(X_1)=0$ and $\det g=1$. The proof of \cref{lem:gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv} then applies, with $E_1$ and \cref{lem:gm_coeff_rho_uy_inv_E} in place of $E_0$ and \cref{lem:gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv_kill}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_conj_diag}]\label{lem:gm_conj_diag}
Assume (R) and (T). Let:
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=\mathrm{diag}(a,b)\in\GL_2(\C)$ with $a\ne0$ and $b\ne0$;
\item $p\ne q$ in $\N^3$;
\item $\kappa,\alpha\in\C$ with $a^{p_0+p_2}b^{p_1+p_2}=\kappa\,a^{q_0+q_2}b^{q_1+q_2}$.
\end{itemize}
Then for every $u\in\C$,
\[
\rho(g)\,\tau_{p,q}(\alpha u)\,\rho(g)^{-1}=\tau_{p,q}(\alpha(\kappa u)).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $W_m=a^{m_0}b^{m_1}(ab)^{m_2}=a^{m_0+m_2}b^{m_1+m_2}$. Then $W_q\ne0$.

By \cref{lem:gm_rho_diag_monomial}, $\rho(g)x^p=W_px^p$. By \cref{lem:gm_coeff_rho_diag} applied to $\rho(g)^{-1}v$, $\cfx{q}{\rho(g)^{-1}v}=W_q^{-1}\cfx{q}{v}$.

\Cref{lem:gm_conj_tau} with $\mu=W_p$ and $\nu=W_q^{-1}$ gives the conjugate $\tau_{p,q}(W_pW_q^{-1}\alpha u)$. Finally, $W_p=\kappa W_q$ by hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_conj_W}]\label{lem:gm_conj_W}
Assume (R) and (T). Let $g=W$, and let $p\ne q$ and $p'\ne q'$ in $\N^3$ with
\[
p'_0=p_1,\quad p'_1=p_0,\quad p'_2=p_2,\qquad q'_0=q_1,\quad q'_1=q_0,\quad q'_2=q_2 .
\]
Let $\alpha,\alpha',\sigma\in\C$ with $(-1)^{p_0}(-1)^{q_0}\alpha=\alpha'\sigma$. Then for every $u\in\C$,
\[
\rho(g)\,\tau_{p,q}(\alpha u)\,\rho(g)^{-1}=\tau_{p',q'}(\alpha'(\sigma u)).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:gm_rho_W_monomial,lem:gm_coeff_rho_W_inv}, \cref{lem:gm_conj_tau} applies with $\mu=(-1)^{p_0}$ and $\nu=(-1)^{q_0}$. It gives $\tau_{p',q'}\bigl((-1)^{p_0}(-1)^{q_0}\alpha u\bigr)=\tau_{p',q'}(\alpha'\sigma u)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_comm_ux}]\label{lem:gm_comm_ux}
Assume (R) and (T). Let $g=\up(t)$, and let $p\ne q$ with $p_1=0$ and $q_0=0$. Then $\rho(g)\tau_{p,q}(u)=\tau_{p,q}(u)\rho(g)$ for every $u\in\C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:gm_rho_ux_monomial,lem:gm_coeff_rho_ux_inv}, \cref{lem:gm_conj_tau} applies with $p'=p$, $q'=q$ and $\mu=\nu=1$. It gives $\rho(g)\tau_{p,q}(u)\rho(g)^{-1}=\tau_{p,q}(u)$; multiply on the right by $\rho(g)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_comm_uy}]\label{lem:gm_comm_uy}
Assume (R) and (T). Let $g=\lo(t)$, and let $p\ne q$ with $p_0=0$ and $q_1=0$. Then $\rho(g)\tau_{p,q}(u)=\tau_{p,q}(u)\rho(g)$ for every $u\in\C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{itemize}
\item $(-1)^{\ell+1}$ is a sign;

\begin{proof}
Write $j=\ell+d+1$. Then $j-\ell-1=j-1-\ell=d$, and
\[
c_{\ell j}=(-1)^{\ell+1}\binom{\ell+d}{\ell}(\ell+1)(d+1),\qquad c_{dj}=(-1)^{d+1}\binom{\ell+d}{d}(d+1)(\ell+1).
\]
Since $\binom{\ell+d}{d}=\binom{\ell+d}{\ell}$, the left side equals
\[
-(-1)^{2\ell+2}(-1)^d\binom{\ell+d}{\ell}(\ell+1)(d+1)=c_{dj}.
\]
The formal proof checks the four parity cases of $\ell$ and $d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_pos_signX}]\label{lem:gm_pos_signX}
For $\ell,a,b\in\N$ with $a=1$ and $b=0$: $(-1)^a(-1)^b\cdot1=(-1)^{\ell+1}(-1)^{\ell}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_pos_signY}]\label{lem:gm_pos_signY}
For $\ell,j,a,b\in\N$ with $a=0$ and $b=1$, and $\kappa\in\C$:
\[
(-1)^a(-1)^b\kappa=-(\kappa(-1)^{j-\ell-1})(-1)^{j-\ell-1}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both sides equal $-\kappa$, since $((-1)^{j-\ell-1})^2=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_pos_signX'}]\label{lem:gm_pos_signX'}
For $\ell,j,a,b\in\N$ with $\ell<j$, $j\le2\ell$, $a=0$ and $b=2\ell-j$:
\[
(-1)^a(-1)^b(-1)^{\ell+1}=1\cdot(-1)^{j-1-\ell}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Under the hypotheses, the subtractions in $\N$ are exact, and
\[
(2\ell-j)+(\ell+1)=(j-1-\ell)+2(2\ell-j+1).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_pos_signY'}]\label{lem:gm_pos_signY'}
For $\ell,j,a,b\in\N$ with $\ell<j$, $j\le2\ell$, $a=2\ell-j$ and $b=0$, and $\kappa\in\C$:
\[
(-1)^a(-1)^b\bigl(-(\kappa(-1)^{j-\ell-1})\bigr)=\kappa(-1)^{j-(j-1-\ell)-1}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First, $j-(j-1-\ell)-1=\ell$. Write $j=\ell+d+1$. Then $j\le2\ell$ gives $\ell=d+e+1$ for some $e$, with $2\ell-j=e$ and $j-\ell-1=d$. Both sides equal $(-1)^{d+e+1}\kappa$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_fam_add}]\label{lem:gm_fam_add}
Let $G$ be supported at $e$ with values $A,A'$. Assume $A(u)A(v)=A(u+v)$ and $A'(u)A'(v)=A'(u+v)$ for all $u,v$. Then $G(g,u)G(g,v)=G(g,u+v)$ for all $g\in E_c$ and $u,v\in\C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Distinguish three cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=e$: this is the hypothesis on $A$;
\item $g=e^*$ (and $g\ne e$): this is the hypothesis on $A'$;
\item otherwise: both sides equal $1$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_fam_conj}]\label{lem:gm_fam_conj}
Let $G$ be supported at $e$ with values $A,A'$. Let $h\in T$ and $\mu\colon E_c\to\C$ satisfy, for all $u$,
\[
hA(u)h^{-1}=A(\mu(e)u),\qquad hA'(u)h^{-1}=A'(\mu(e^*)u).
\]
Then $hG(g,u)h^{-1}=G(g,\mu(g)u)$ for all $g\in E_c$ and $u\in\C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Distinguish three cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item $g=e$: the hypothesis on $A$, together with $G(e^*,\cdot)=A'$.
\item $g=e^*$: the hypothesis on $A'$, together with $(e^*)^*=e$ (\cref{lem:gm_refl_refl}) and $G(e,\cdot)=A$.
\item Otherwise: the left side is $1$. Moreover $g^*\ne e$ (else $g=g^{**}=e^*$) and $g^*\ne e^*$ (else $g=e$), both by \cref{lem:gm_refl_refl}. So the right side is also $1$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_fam_comm1}]\label{lem:gm_fam_comm1}
Let $G$ be supported at $e$ with values $A,A'$. Let $h\colon\C\to T$ and let $\mathsf P$ be a property of indices. Assume:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\mathsf P(e)$, then $h(u)A(v)=A(v)h(u)$ for all $u,v$;
\item if $\mathsf P(e^*)$, then $h(u)A'(v)=A'(v)h(u)$ for all $u,v$.
\end{itemize}
Then $h(u)G(g,v)=G(g,v)h(u)$ for every $g$ with $\mathsf P(g)$ and all $u,v$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_fam_U2}]\label{lem:gm_fam_U2}
Let $G$ be supported at $e$ with values $A,A'$, and let $H\colon E_c\times\C\to T$ be supported at $e$ with values $B,B'$. Assume:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $1<|\ell(e)-\ell(e^*)|$, then $A(u)B'(v)=B'(v)A(u)$ for all $u,v$;
\item if $1<|\ell(e^*)-\ell(e)|$, then $A'(u)B(v)=B(v)A'(u)$ for all $u,v$.
\end{itemize}
Then $G(f,u)H(g,v)=H(g,v)G(f,u)$ for all $u,v$ and all $f,g\in E_c$ such that $j(f)\ne j(g)$, or $k(f)\ne k(g)$, or $1<|\ell(f)-\ell(g)|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $f\notin\{e,e^*\}$, then $G(f,u)=1$, and similarly for $g$ and $H$. It remains to consider $f,g\in\{e,e^*\}$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $f=g$, the side condition fails, since $j$, $k$ and $\ell$ all agree.
\item Otherwise $\{f,g\}=\{e,e^*\}$ with $f\ne g$. Since $e$ and $e^*$ have the same $j$ and $k$, the side condition forces $|\ell(f)-\ell(g)|>1$. The two hypotheses cover $(f,g)=(e,e^*)$ and $(f,g)=(e^*,e)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_fam_XY}]\label{lem:gm_fam_XY}
Let $G$ and $H$ be supported at $e$ with values $A,A'$ and $B,B'$ respectively. Write $c_g:=c_{\ell(g)j(g)}$. Assume that for all $s,t\in\C^\times$
\[
B(-t)A(s)B(t)=A(-t^{-1}/c_e)\,B(-c_et^2s)\,A(t^{-1}/c_e),
\]
and likewise for $A',B'$ with $c_{e^*}$. Then for all $g\in E_c$ and $s,t\in\C^\times$,
\[
H(g,-t)G(g,s)H(g,t)=G(g,-t^{-1}/c_g)\,H(g,-c_gt^2s)\,G(g,t^{-1}/c_g).
\]
\end{lemma}

For $g=e$ and $g=e^*$ this is the hypothesis. For any other $g$, all six factors are $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{gm_rel_of}]\label{lem:gm_rel_of}
Let $T$ be a group, $F\colon\Gen_c\to T$, $\rho\colon\GL_2(\C)\to T$ a group homomorphism, and $f_0\colon\Gen_c\to\GL_2(\C)$ with $\overline{f_0}(r)=1$ for all $r\in\mathcal R_c$. Write $c_g:=c_{\ell(g)j(g)}$. Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $F(z)=\rho(f_0(z))$ for every $z$ of the form $H_1(s)$, $H_2(s)$, $X_{-1}(u)$, $Y_{-1}(u)$.
\item For all $g\in E_c$ and $u,v\in\C$: $F(X_g(u))F(X_g(v))=F(X_g(u+v))$ and $F(Y_g(u))F(Y_g(v))=F(Y_g(u+v))$.
\item For all $g\in E_c$ and $s,t\in\C^\times$:
\[
F(Y_g(-t))F(X_g(s))F(Y_g(t))=F(X_g(-t^{-1}/c_g))\,F(Y_g(-c_gt^2s))\,F(X_g(t^{-1}/c_g)).
\]
\item For all $s\in\C^\times$, $g\in E_c$ and $u\in\C$, conjugation by $F(H_1(s))$ and $F(H_2(s))$ sends:
\begin{itemize}
\item $F(X_g(u))$ to $F(X_g(s^{\ell(g)+1}u))$ and $F(X_g(s^{j(g)-\ell(g)}u))$ respectively;
\item $F(Y_g(u))$ to $F(Y_g((s^{-1})^{\ell(g)+1}u))$ and $F(Y_g((s^{-1})^{j(g)-\ell(g)}u))$ respectively.
\end{itemize}
\item For all $u,v$:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\ell(g)=j(g)-1$, then $F(X_{-1}(u))$ commutes with $F(X_g(v))$, and $F(Y_{-1}(u))$ commutes with $F(Y_g(v))$;
\item if $\ell(g)=0$, then $F(Y_{-1}(u))$ commutes with $F(X_g(v))$, and $F(X_{-1}(u))$ commutes with $F(Y_g(v))$.
\end{itemize}
\item For all $f,g\in E_c$ with $j(f)\ne j(g)$, or $k(f)\ne k(g)$, or $1<|\ell(f)-\ell(g)|$, and all $u,v$: $F(X_f(u))$ commutes with $F(Y_g(v))$.
\item With $\omega:=F(X_{-1}(1))F(Y_{-1}(-1))F(X_{-1}(1))$, for all $g$ and $u$:
\[
\omega F(X_g(u))\omega^{-1}=F(X_{g^*}((-1)^{\ell(g)}u)),\qquad \omega F(Y_g(u))\omega^{-1}=F(Y_{g^*}((-1)^{j(g)-\ell(g)-1}u)).
\]
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Argue by cases on the relation family.

The sixteen families (H:1a), (H:1b), (H:2), (Re:1a)--(Re:6d) and (U:5a) involve only the generators $H_1,H_2,X_{-1},Y_{-1}$. For such a relator $r$, hypothesis 1 and the homomorphism property of $\rho$ give $\overline F(r)=\rho(\overline{f_0}(r))=\rho(1)=1$.

For every other family, the image of the relator is $ab^{-1}$ or a commutator in $T$. The corresponding hypothesis (2--7) says exactly that $a=b$, or that the two elements commute. For (U:4a,b), note that $\wt_{-1}=X_{-1}(1)Y_{-1}(-1^{-1})X_{-1}(1)$ with $1^{-1}=1$ in $\C^\times$, so $\overline F(\wt_{-1})=\omega$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Fix $c\colon\N\to\N$. The first four claims are \cref{lem:setting_real_part_nontrivial}. It remains to prove that $X_e(u)\ne1$ and $Y_e(u)\ne1$ for $e\in E_c$ and $u\ne0$.

\emph{Step 1: the $\GL_2$-realization.}
Let $f_0$ be the map of \cref{lem:gm_gl2_rel_aux}. By \cref{lem:gm_gl2_rel}, $\overline{f_0}$ kills every relator.

\emph{Step 2: the action on $P$.}
For $g\in\GL_2(\C)$, \cref{lem:gm_aeval_subst_mul,lem:gm_aeval_subst_one} give
\[
\sigma_g\sigma_{g^{-1}}=\sigma_1=\mathrm{id}=\sigma_{g^{-1}}\sigma_g .
\]
So $\sigma_g\in\Aut(P)$. By \cref{lem:gm_aeval_subst_mul}, $\rho(g):=\sigma_g$ is a homomorphism. Thus (R) holds.

\emph{Step 3: transvections.}
For $p\ne q$ put $\tau_{p,q}(u)=\mathrm{id}+uN_{p,q}$, where $N_{p,q}(f)=\cfx{q}{f}x^p$. Its inverse is $\mathrm{id}-uN_{p,q}$ by \cref{lem:gm_L_inv}. For $p=q$ put $\tau_{p,q}(u)=1$. Thus (T) holds.

\emph{Step 4: the main claim.}
Let $e=(\ell,j,k)\in E_c$, write $\ell^*=\ell(e^*)=j-1-\ell$, and for $m\in\N^3$ let $\bar m=(m_1,m_0,m_2)$. Suppose $p,q,p',q'\in\N^3$ and $\alpha,\beta,\alpha',\beta'\in\C$ satisfy:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $p\ne q$ and $p'\ne q'$.
\item[(ii)] $\alpha\beta=c_{\ell j}$ and $\alpha'\beta'=c_{\ell^*j}$.
\item[(iii)] The weight conditions
\begin{align*}
p_0+p_2&=q_0+q_2+\ell+1, & p_1+p_2&=q_1+q_2+(j-\ell),\\
p'_0+p'_2&=q'_0+q'_2+\ell^*+1, & p'_1+p'_2&=q'_1+q'_2+(j-\ell^*).
\end{align*}
\item[(iv)] $p'=\bar p$ and $q'=\bar q$, coordinatewise.
\item[(v)] The sign conditions
\begin{align*}
(-1)^{p_0}(-1)^{q_0}\alpha&=\alpha'(-1)^{\ell}, & (-1)^{q_0}(-1)^{p_0}\beta&=\beta'(-1)^{j-\ell-1},\\
(-1)^{p'_0}(-1)^{q'_0}\alpha'&=\alpha(-1)^{\ell^*}, & (-1)^{q'_0}(-1)^{p'_0}\beta'&=\beta(-1)^{j-\ell^*-1}.
\end{align*}
\item[(vi)] The vanishing conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell=j-1\Rightarrow p_1=q_0=0$;
\item $\ell=0\Rightarrow p_0=q_1=0$;
\item $\ell^*=j-1\Rightarrow p'_1=q'_0=0$;
\item $\ell^*=0\Rightarrow p'_0=q'_1=0$.
\end{itemize}
\item[(vii)] $1<|\ell-\ell^*|\Rightarrow p\ne p'$ and $q\ne q'$.
\item[(viii)] $e^*=e\Rightarrow p'=p$, $q'=q$, $\alpha'=\alpha$ and $\beta'=\beta$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Claim:} under (i)--(viii), for every $u\ne0$, the elements $X_e(u)$, $Y_e(u)$, $X_{e^*}(u)$ and $Y_{e^*}(u)$ of $\Gm(c)$ are all $\ne1$.

\emph{Proof of the claim.}
By \cref{lem:gm_cst_ne_zero}, $c_{\ell j}\ne0$ and $c_{\ell^*j}\ne0$, so $\alpha,\beta,\alpha',\beta'\ne0$ by (ii).

Define $F\colon\Gen_c\to\Aut(P)$ by:
\begin{itemize}
\item $F(z)=\rho(f_0(z))$ for $z$ among $H_1(s),H_2(s),X_{-1}(u),Y_{-1}(u)$;
\item $F(X_g(u))=\tau_{p,q}(\alpha u)$ if $g=e$, $\tau_{p',q'}(\alpha'u)$ if $g=e^*\ne e$, and $1$ otherwise;
\item $F(Y_g(u))=\tau_{q,p}(\beta u)$ if $g=e$, $\tau_{q',p'}(\beta'u)$ if $g=e^*\ne e$, and $1$ otherwise.
\end{itemize}
By (viii), $F(X_{e^*}(u))=\tau_{p',q'}(\alpha'u)$ and $F(Y_{e^*}(u))=\tau_{q',p'}(\beta'u)$ also hold when $e^*=e$. Hence $(g,u)\mapsto F(X_g(u))$ is supported at $e$ with values $\tau_{p,q}(\alpha\,\cdot)$ and $\tau_{p',q'}(\alpha'\,\cdot)$. Likewise $(g,u)\mapsto F(Y_g(u))$ is supported at $e$ with values $\tau_{q,p}(\beta\,\cdot)$ and $\tau_{q',p'}(\beta'\,\cdot)$.

By \cref{lem:gm_weyl_matrix},
\[
\omega=F(X_{-1}(1))F(Y_{-1}(-1))F(X_{-1}(1))=\rho\bigl(f_0(X_{-1}(1))f_0(Y_{-1}(-1))f_0(X_{-1}(1))\bigr)=\rho(g_W)
\]
with $g_W=W$.

We verify the hypotheses of \cref{lem:gm_rel_of}, with $T=\Aut(P)$, $\rho$ and $f_0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Hypothesis 1 holds by definition, and $\overline{f_0}$ kills $\mathcal R_c$ by Step 1.
\item Hypothesis 2: \cref{lem:gm_fam_add}, with additivity from \cref{lem:gm_tau_add} and (i).
\item Hypothesis 3: \cref{lem:gm_fam_XY}, with the two inputs from \cref{lem:gm_tau_sl2}. Take $(a,b,\kappa)=(\alpha,\beta,c_{\ell j})$ for $p,q$ and $(\alpha',\beta',c_{\ell^*j})$ for $p',q'$; these satisfy the hypotheses by (ii).
\item Hypothesis 4: \cref{lem:gm_fam_conj}, with $h=F(H_i(s))=\rho(\mathrm{diag}(s,1))$ or $\rho(\mathrm{diag}(1,s))$, and the inputs from \cref{lem:gm_conj_diag}.
\begin{itemize}
\item For $X$ with $H_1$: $\mu(g)=s^{\ell(g)+1}$. The required weight identity $s^{p_0+p_2}=\kappa s^{q_0+q_2}$ with $\kappa=s^{\ell+1}$ is (iii), and the same for $p',q'$.
\item For $X$ with $H_2$: $\mu(g)=s^{j(g)-\ell(g)}$, again by (iii).
\item For $Y$, the roles of $p$ and $q$ are exchanged, and $\kappa=(s^{-1})^{\ell+1}$ or $(s^{-1})^{j-\ell}$. The weight identity becomes $s^{q_0+q_2}=(s^{\ell+1})^{-1}s^{q_0+q_2+\ell+1}$, which is \cref{lem:gm_pow_inv_mul}.
\end{itemize}
\item Hypothesis 5: \cref{lem:gm_fam_comm1} with $\mathsf P(g)$ equal to $\ell(g)=j(g)-1$ or $\ell(g)=0$. The inputs come from \cref{lem:gm_comm_ux} (for $h=\rho(\up(u))$) and \cref{lem:gm_comm_uy} (for $h=\rho(\lo(u))$), applied to $(p,q)$ or $(q,p)$ and their primed versions. The required vanishing of exponents is (vi).
\item Hypothesis 6: \cref{lem:gm_fam_U2}, with the inputs from \cref{lem:gm_tau_comm}. The required inequalities $p\ne p'$ and $q\ne q'$ are (vii). The second input uses $|\ell^*-\ell|=|\ell-\ell^*|$.
\item Hypothesis 7: \cref{lem:gm_fam_weyl} with $h=\omega=\rho(g_W)$, and the inputs from \cref{lem:gm_conj_W}.
\begin{itemize}
\item For $X$: $\mu(g)=(-1)^{\ell(g)}$. Use \cref{lem:gm_conj_W} for $(p,q)\to(p',q')$ with $\sigma=(-1)^{\ell}$, and for $(p',q')\to(p,q)$ with $\sigma=(-1)^{\ell^*}$. The swap conditions are (iv), read in both directions; the sign conditions are the first column of (v).
\item For $Y$: $\mu(g)=(-1)^{j(g)-\ell(g)-1}$. Use the same lemma for $(q,p)\to(q',p')$ and back, with the second column of (v).
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
Hence $\overline F$ kills $\mathcal R_c$. By the universal property of the presented group there is a homomorphism $\varphi\colon\Gm(c)\to\Aut(P)$ with $\varphi(z)=F(z)$ on generators. If $z=1$ in $\Gm(c)$, then $F(z)=1$.

Finally, let $u\ne0$. Then $\alpha u$, $\beta u$, $\alpha'u$ and $\beta'u$ are non-zero. By \cref{lem:gm_tau_ne_one} and (i), the four transvections $F(X_e(u))$, $F(Y_e(u))$, $F(X_{e^*}(u))$ and $F(Y_{e^*}(u))$ are $\ne1$. This proves the claim.

\emph{Step 5: the case $j\le2\ell$.}
Apply the claim with
\[
p=(1,0,\ell),\quad q=(0,2\ell-j,0),\quad p'=(0,1,\ell),\quad q'=(2\ell-j,0,0),
\]
and
\[
\alpha=1,\quad\beta=c_{\ell j},\quad\alpha'=(-1)^{\ell+1},\quad\beta'=-c_{\ell j}(-1)^{j-\ell-1}.
\]
In monomials, $x^p=X_0Z^\ell$, $x^q=X_1^{2\ell-j}$, $x^{p'}=X_1Z^\ell$ and $x^{q'}=X_0^{2\ell-j}$. Recall $\ell^*=j-1-\ell$. We check (i)--(viii).
\begin{itemize}
\item (i): $p_0\ne q_0$ and $p'_1\ne q'_1$.
\item (ii): $\alpha\beta=c_{\ell j}$ trivially, and $\alpha'\beta'=c_{\ell^* j}$ by \cref{lem:gm_pos_cst}.
\item (iii): $1+\ell=\ell+1$; $\ell=(2\ell-j)+(j-\ell)$; $\ell=(2\ell-j)+\ell^*+1$; $1+\ell=j-\ell^*$. All use $\ell<j\le2\ell$.
\item (iv): immediate.
\item (v): \cref{lem:gm_pos_signX,lem:gm_pos_signY,lem:gm_pos_signX',lem:gm_pos_signY'}, with $(p_0,q_0)=(1,0)$ and $(p'_0,q'_0)=(0,2\ell-j)$.
\item (vi):
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\ell=j-1$, then $p_1=q_0=0$;
\item $\ell=0$ is impossible, as it would force $j\le0$;
\item $\ell^*=j-1$ means $\ell=0$, again impossible;
\item if $\ell^*=0$, then $p'_0=q'_1=0$.
\end{itemize}
\item (vii): $p_0\ne p'_0$. If $|\ell-\ell^*|=|2\ell-j+1|>1$, then $2\ell-j\ge1$, so $q_1\ne q'_1$.
\item (viii): $e^*=e$ would give $\ell=j-1-\ell$, contradicting $j\le2\ell$.
\end{itemize}
Hence $X_e(u),Y_e(u),X_{e^*}(u),Y_{e^*}(u)\ne1$ for $u\ne0$.

\emph{Step 6: the case $j=2\ell+1$.}
Here $\ell^*=\ell$, $j-\ell-1=\ell$ and $e^*=e$. Apply the claim with $p=p'=(\ell,\ell,1)$, $q=q'=0$, $\alpha=\alpha'=1$ and $\beta=\beta'=c_{\ell j}$; that is, $x^p=(X_0X_1)^\ell Z$ and $x^q=1$.
\begin{itemize}
\item (i): $p_2=1\ne0=q_2$.
\item (ii): immediate, since $c_{\ell^*j}=c_{\ell j}$.
\item (iii): $\ell+1=\ell+1$ and $\ell+1=j-\ell$.
\item (iv): $p$ and $0$ are swap-invariant.
\item (v): every equation reduces to $(-1)^\ell\alpha=\alpha(-1)^\ell$ or $(-1)^\ell\beta=\beta(-1)^\ell$.
\item (vi): $\ell=j-1$ or $\ell=0$ both force $\ell=0$, so $p_0=p_1=0=q_0=q_1$.
\item (vii): vacuous, since $|\ell-\ell|=0$.
\item (viii): immediate.
\end{itemize}
Hence $X_e(u),Y_e(u)\ne1$ for $u\ne0$.

\emph{Step 7: conclusion.}
Let $e\in E_c$ and $u\ne0$, and compare $2\ell+1$ with $j$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $2\ell+1>j$, then $j\le2\ell$, and Step 5 applies to $e$.
\item If $2\ell+1=j$, Step 6 applies.
\item If $2\ell+1<j$, then $e^*$ satisfies $j\le2(j-1-\ell)$. Step 5 applied to $e^*$ gives the result for $(e^*)^*$, which equals $e$ by \cref{lem:gm_refl_refl}.
\end{itemize}
Together with the first four claims, this proves all six statements.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The proof never uses the values of $c$, the constraint $j=2\ell+1$, or the removal of any relation. In particular (Im:2) is kept, with the constant $c_{\ell j}$ as defined. The homomorphisms used are different for different indices $e$: each one detects only the generators indexed by $e$ and $e^*$, together with the real generators. This suffices for the statement, which concerns each generator separately.
\end{remark}

\section{Independent review}

A referee model (claude-opus-5-5), which took no part in the formalization or the proof, compared the verified Lean file with the source. Verdict: \textbf{FAITHFUL}.

\paragraph{Definitions.} I checked each declaration of the target file against the source presentation.

\begin{itemize}
\item \leanname{EIdx} encodes $E=\{(\ell,j,k)\mid j\in\mathbb{N},\ 1\le k\le c(j),\ 0\le\ell<j\}$ through the fields \leanname{hk1}, \leanname{hkc} and \leanname{hl}. Here $c:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is arbitrary, as the formalization notes allow.
\item \leanname{EIdx.refl} sends $(\ell,j,k)\mapsto(j-1-\ell,j,k)$. With $\ell<j$ the truncated subtraction is exact. This is the index map used in (U:4).
\item \leanname{Gen} has one constructor per symbol family of $\mathcal{X}$: $H_1(s)$ and $H_2(s)$ with $s\in\mathbb{C}^\times$, and $X_{-1}$, $Y_{-1}$, $X_{\ell,jk}$, $Y_{\ell,jk}$ with arguments in $\mathbb{C}$.
\item \leanname{cst} is $(-1)^{\ell+1}\binom{j-1}{\ell}(\ell+1)(j-\ell)$, which is $c_{\ell j}$.
\item \leanname{wt} and \leanname{w} are the abbreviations (Re:0). They are words in the free group, not generators. \leanname{comm} is $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$; the convention is irrelevant for relations of the form $=1$.
\item \leanname{Rel} has one constructor per relation family: H:1a, H:1b, H:2; Re:1a through Re:6d; Im:1a, Im:1b, Im:2, Im:6a--d; U:1a--d; U:2; U:4a, U:4b; U:5a. None is missing and none is extra. Each relation $a=b$ is encoded as $ab^{-1}$.
\item I checked the arguments of each constructor against the source.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item In \leanname{XY} the term \texttt{-(t:C)\^{}2 * s} parses as $-(t^2)s$, as in the source.
  \item This parse is also confirmed by the proof. The proof checks the relation with the standard matrices, and a direct computation gives $Y(-t)X(s)Y(t)=X(-t^{-1})Y(-t^2s)X(t^{-1})$ for those matrices.
  \item \leanname{ImXY} has $X(-t^{-1}/c_{\ell j})\,Y(-c_{\ell j}t^2s)\,X(t^{-1}/c_{\ell j})$, matching the source.
  \item The exponents in Im:6 are $s^{\ell+1}$, $s^{j-\ell}$, $(s^{-1})^{\ell+1}$ and $(s^{-1})^{j-\ell}$, matching the source.
  \item The side conditions of U:1a--d are $\ell=j-1$ or $\ell=0$, as in the source.
  \item The side condition of U:2 is $j\ne p\vee k\ne q\vee|\ell-m|>1$, as in the source.
  \item The signs in U:4 are $(-1)^{\ell}$ and $(-1)^{j-\ell-1}$, as in the source.
  \item U:5a is $Y(s)=X(s^{-1})H_1(-s^{-1})H_2(-s)\,\widetilde w_{-1}\,X(s^{-1})$, as in the source.
  \end{itemize}
\item Quantification follows the source: $s,t\in\mathbb{C}^\times$ and $u,v\in\mathbb{C}$.
\item \leanname{Gm} is the presented group on this relator set. The relator set is not degenerate.
\end{itemize}
I found no discrepancy. The authors' optional modifications were not used: the constraint $j=2\ell+1$ is not added, and Im:2 is not removed.

\paragraph{Statement.} The target statement has six conjuncts:
\begin{itemize}
\item $X_{-1}(u)\ne1$ and $Y_{-1}(u)\ne1$ for $u\ne0$;
\item $H_1(s)\ne1$ and $H_2(s)\ne1$ for $s\in\mathbb{C}^\times$ with $s\ne1$;
\item $X_{\ell,jk}(u)\ne1$ and $Y_{\ell,jk}(u)\ne1$ for every index in $E$ and every $u\ne0$.
\end{itemize}
These are exactly the source's six claims, stated in $\mathrm{Gm}\,c$.

The statement is quantified over all $c:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$. It therefore implies the source's case where $c(j)$ are the coefficients of $J$; nothing extra needs to be supplied.

On edge inputs:
\begin{itemize}
\item For $j=0$, $E$ has no elements, as in the source.
\item If $c$ were identically zero, the last two conjuncts would be vacuous. They are not vacuous for the source's $c$, and they are proved uniformly in $c$.
\end{itemize}

Answer to the authors' question: no generator family collapses. All six families survive, with the full index set and with Im:2 retained.

\paragraph{Proof.} \begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Real part.} \leanname{setting_real_part_nontrivial} maps the generators to $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{C})$:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $H_1(s)\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(s,1)$ and $H_2(s)\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(1,s)$;
  \item $X_{-1}(u)$ and $Y_{-1}(u)$ map to the upper and lower unipotent matrices;
  \item all imaginary generators map to $1$.
  \end{itemize}
  Every relator is checked to map to $1$ by matrix computation. The images of the real generators are visibly nontrivial, which gives the first four conjuncts.
\item \textbf{Imaginary part.} For each index $e$ the proof builds a representation on the vector space $\mathbb{C}[X_0,X_1,Z]$. The pieces are as follows.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $\rho$ is the substitution action of $\mathrm{GL}_2$, with $Z$ scaled by the determinant.
  \item $\tau_{p,q}(u)$ is the monomial transvection $v\mapsto v+u\,\mathrm{coeff}_q(v)\,m_p$.
  \item The representation sends $X_e(u)\mapsto\tau_{p,q}(\alpha u)$ and $Y_e(u)\mapsto\tau_{q,p}(\beta u)$, with $\alpha\beta=c_{\ell j}$.
  \item $X_{e.\mathrm{refl}}$ and $Y_{e.\mathrm{refl}}$ map to the analogous transvections on the Weyl-swapped monomials.
  \item All other imaginary generators map to $1$.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{The general lemma.} \leanname{general} derives every relation from a short list of arithmetic side conditions:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item weight conditions on the monomials, giving Im:6;
  \item sign conditions, giving U:4;
  \item vanishing of exponents, giving U:1;
  \item $p\ne p'$ and $q\ne q'$, giving U:2;
  \item an $\mathrm{SL}_2$ identity for transvections with $\alpha\beta=c_{\ell j}\ne0$, giving Im:2.
  \end{itemize}
  The real relations are inherited from the $\mathrm{GL}_2$ check via \leanname{gm_gl2_rel} and \leanname{gm_rel_of}.
\item \textbf{Choice of monomials.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For $j\le2\ell$ the proof takes $p=X_0Z^{\ell}$ and $q=X_1^{2\ell-j}$, together with their swaps.
  \item For $j=2\ell+1$ it takes $p=(X_0X_1)^{\ell}Z$ and $q=1$. In this case $e.\mathrm{refl}=e$.
  \item The case $j>2\ell+1$ is reduced to the first case through $e.\mathrm{refl}$.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Nontriviality.} \leanname{gm_tau_ne_one} shows that $\tau_{p,q}(u)\ne1$ for $u\ne0$.
\end{itemize}

The source gives no proof. This argument is the homomorphism-to-a-concrete-group method suggested in the task note. It is legitimate, uses no extra hypotheses, and I found no lemma whose statement is weaker than needed.

\paragraph{Concerns.} \begin{itemize}
\item The value of $c$ plays no role: the theorem is proved for arbitrary $c$, which is stronger than the source needs.
\item The constructed representations act on the infinite-dimensional space $\mathbb{C}[X_0,X_1,Z]$. Only group homomorphisms are needed, so this does not affect validity.
\end{itemize}
